planting.note: Direct sow in fall so seed overwinters naturally, or set divisions in spring into well-drained meadow or streamside soil; this West Coast native spreads readily by rhizome once established.

directions: Native to coastal prairies, grasslands, and streambanks from British Columbia south through California, Pacific aster produces masses of lavender to pale-purple, yellow-centered daisy flowers from midsummer into fall. It tolerates both seasonal drought and periodic flooding once its root system is established, and performs well in clay or saline-influenced soils where many other perennials struggle. Give it room to spread, since vigorous rhizomes can form sizeable colonies in moist, sunny sites. Late-season bloom makes it valuable for migrating pollinators along the Pacific flyway.

planting.note: Direct sow outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil; space to allow for rhizome spread.

directions: A Pacific Northwest native found from coastal bluffs and salt marshes to damp forest clearings and streamside meadows, Douglas aster bears violet-blue, yellow-centered flowers from late summer through mid-fall. It handles salt spray, seasonal flooding, and heavy wet soils better than most garden asters, spreading gradually by rhizome into substantial colonies. Plant it in sun to light shade along pond margins, rain gardens, or coastal plantings where other perennials struggle with excess moisture. Its late bloom is an important nectar source for migrating butterflies in the maritime Northwest.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for cold stratification, or set divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich woodland soil at mid-to-high elevation sites with dappled light.

directions: Also known by the older synonym Aster curtisii, whitetop aster is a Southern Appalachian specialty found in moist woodlands, open oak-pine stands, and shaded roadbanks at moderate to high elevations in Virginia, the Carolinas, Georgia, Tennessee, and Alabama. From August into October it produces pale blue to violet ray flowers with cream-to-pink disk centers above slightly nodding stems. It thrives in the dappled light of mountain woodland edges and is a good choice for naturalistic shade gardens at higher elevation or in cooler climates where many sun-loving asters struggle. Late bloom provides nectar for fall-migrating pollinators in the mountain understory.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, rocky, well-drained soil for winter stratification; avoid rich or heavily amended beds, which favor taller competitors over this diminutive barrens specialist.

directions: Serpentine aster, also called starved aster, is a small, delicate wildflower restricted to thin, mineral-rich serpentine and diabase barrens in southeastern Pennsylvania, Maryland, and a disjunct outlier in north-central North Carolina. Its wiry stems carry numerous small white-rayed flower heads in late summer and early fall, well below the height of most garden asters. Because it is adapted to the lean, droughty, rocky soils of its native barrens, it resents fertile garden beds and competition from larger neighbors, making it best suited to rock gardens or barrens-restoration plantings that mimic its harsh natural habitat. Give it full sun and sharp drainage and leave it undisturbed once established.

planting.note: Direct sow or set container plants into lean, well-drained, sandy flatwoods soil in full sun; cold-stratify seed before spring sowing to improve germination.

directions: Savanna blazing star is a rare gayfeather endemic to mesic pine flatwoods of a handful of counties along Florida's southwest Gulf coast, where it is ranked vulnerable due to its restricted range. Tall, wand-like spikes of rosy-purple button flowers appear in fall, later than many other blazing stars, offering late-season nectar as migrating monarchs pass through peninsular Florida. It is a relatively short-lived perennial in cultivation and its flowering stalks can grow top-heavy; cutting plants back by a third in midsummer helps keep them upright. Plant it in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to mimic the open flatwoods conditions it requires.
